copy.caption:
Every house has one room nobody can name. The listing photo has to call it something, and whatever you call it is what the buyer prices.

Empty, that room is a question. We staged the same photograph three times and never moved the camera.

As an office it sells to the buyer who works from home. As a guest room it sells to the buyer whose family visits. As a reading room it sells to the buyer who wants somewhere quiet. Same walls, same window, same floor. Three different buyers.

Go and look at your own gallery. If a room in it has no furniture and no label, the buyer is filling it in for you, and they will fill it in with the version they do not want.

copy.headline: 97% of agents say curb appeal brings the buyer.
copy.caption:
The exterior is the first photo in the listing. It is also the only one nobody restages.

97% of agents told NAR that curb appeal matters for attracting a buyer. Three quarters of them called it very important. Not somewhat. Very.

Then the photo goes up shot at noon under a flat grey sky, because that is when the appointment was.

This is the same photograph. Same house, same brick, same hedge, same neighbour's roofline in the corner. Golden hour and a clear sky, applied as a preset. Nothing was added to the property and nothing was taken away from it except the parked cars and the bins.

That is the whole job. You are not renovating anything. You are photographing it on the day it looks like itself.

First render is free.

Source: NAR, 2023 Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features.

The property is preserved exactly against the source: same brick courses, same arched window mullions, same entry canopy, same porch lamp, same hedge line, same neighbour's roof in the corner. Attempt 2 scored 80 against attempt 1's 85 and was discarded.

generation.authorNote: This post does not use acquirePair. Both of acquireBefore's screens reject a curb-appeal photograph by construction: validateSource is the INTERIOR upload gate, which answers 'not a room' at a facade and 'vehicle' when there is a car on the drive, and fitsBrief hardcodes 'Reject it if it is an exterior' in its screening prompt, so no brief wording gets past it. posts/_work/build-0815.mjs writes the sourcing loop out with the exterior gate substituted, keeping the content-addressed store, the never-reuse-a-source rule and the two-source retry. Two additive passthroughs were added to lib/images/stagify.js: reviewBasePrompt, so a facade is not graded against 'warped furniture' and 'extra legs', and validateExteriorSource. The product's own exterior route sets skipQualityReview because a retry gives a waiting customer a different sky rather than a better one; this kept the loop on, because rule 3 is about the advertisement and not about the wait.

round1Blocking: The roof was re-materialised: the source shingle is dark charcoal whose hip ridge caps and dormer roofs read LIGHTER than the field, and the render turned the field warm tan and drove the caps and dormers to near black, inverting the relationship rather than warming it.
A tall capped metal flue was invented on the main hip ridge, where the source has only a low flat ridge vent further down the same hip.
review.howFixed: Not fixed, and shipped anyway with the user's approval after the two-round cap. Round two named both failure modes inside additionalPrompt, which buildExteriorPrompt appends as the highest priority clause in the prompt. It did not restore the charcoal roof, and it added lit interior windows the source does not have, so it was the worse of the two. THE REASON THIS IS SHIPPABLE IS THE CROP, and nothing else: .band shows the facade only, and the entire main roofline including both defects is outside it. The reviewer confirmed the property IS preserved within the published crop, checking brick courses, window count, mullion pattern, entry canopy, porch lamp, downpipes, hedge line and the neighbouring house against the source. Anyone reusing this render at full size, or cropping it higher, inherits a roof that misstates the product. It is kept in the record rather than deleted so that fact is visible.
review.nextTimeTry: goldenHour appears to be what drives the warm cast across the whole roof. midday plus clearBlue is the preset pair to try first on a charcoal roofed property, or source a house whose roof is already warm toned so the failure mode cannot arise.
nits: A small dark block hangs below the right end of the second floor window sill, with a smeared wedge running off the sill into the brick. Nothing corresponds to it in the source. Present in the published crop, sub legible at feed size.
The stone jamb and arch haunch of that same window lose their block joints to a soft grey blur, where the source has crisp quoins.
The GOLDEN HOUR pill sits on the most shadowed part of the band, so the label is contradicted by the pixels immediately around it.
The band crop shows no curb, front yard or landscaping, which is a gap for a post whose headline is about curb appeal. stat-card has one photo slot and the sky and facade were the higher priority.
Headline line three is the orphan word 'buyer.'
The CTA pill leaves 32px at the bottom against 64px on the other three sides.
review.haloVerdict: The automated QA flagged a roofline halo twice and scored 85. Measured against the source it is a 3 to 5 level luminance lift out of 255 in the sky approaching the roof, under 2 percent, and the source itself already carries the same 2 to 3 pixel bright rim from ordinary lens and JPEG edge softness. It does not survive at feed size and the only roof to sky boundary reaching the published image is the neighbour's gable, which shows none. Not a shipping problem.
review.dashAudit: Zero dash-like characters of any kind across all nine text runs. No hyphen, figure dash, en dash, em dash, minus sign or horizontal bar appears anywhere, so there was no glyph to measure against a lowercase n. The percent sign's bar is a diagonal about 55 degrees off horizontal and does not read as a dash. The only horizontal strokes in the frame are photographic: the overhead cables, the window transom bars and the stone sill line.
review.samenessVerdict: Not a rerun. All five recent posts are interiors sold on a full bleed or split photograph, and four of the five are a before and after divided by a seam. This is the only exterior, the only frame led by a large numeral, the only one where the deep blue ground is the dominant surface with the photograph demoted to a letterboxed band, and the only one carrying a cited statistic and a source line. Colour separates it too: orange brick and gold against navy, against a recent run of cool grey, warm beige and coastal aqua.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: Chosen by the user over the advocate's pick. Curb appeal is under-posted, it is the one staging job the design audience will argue about, and Outdoors keeps every chair out of frame so the known extra-leg artifact cannot touch the render.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The band shows only the after. stat-card has one photo slot, so the relight is named by the GOLDEN HOUR pill and carried by the caption rather than shown as a pair. A reader who does not read the caption sees a nice photograph of a house and has to take the change on trust.
devilsAdvocate.authorNote: The advocate's central attack on i06 was that 'The first photo gets 3 seconds' is an invented figure, and stat-card's own rules say never invent one. A researcher subagent confirmed it: the seconds figure has no traceable primary source, drifts between 1, 2, 5 and 8 across vendor blogs that cite each other, and where a paper is named it is Seiler 2012, which does not appear to state it. The headline was replaced with a number pulled verbatim from NAR's own PDF. The 7% sale-price figure from JREFE was the alternative and was rejected for display size: the paper says UP TO 7% and bundles the seller's curb appeal with the across-the-street neighbour's, which a 280px numeral cannot hedge. The 2018 NAR '87% of buyers find photos very useful' was rejected as stale; NAR's own 2025 figure is 83%. The claim line says agents rather than buyers because that is what the survey measured.

copy.headline: Free is not a teaser.
copy.caption:
Free virtual staging usually means a watermarked preview. Ours means the file you put on the listing.

The kitchen in this post was rendered on the free tier. Not a screenshot from the paid plan, not a demo account. The free one.

What free includes:

All eight room types. Bedroom, living room, dining room, kitchen, office, bathroom, outdoors and dorm.
All seven style presets.
The full size file, with no watermark on it.
No card to start.

What it does not:

Stagify+ is $11.99 a month. It adds furniture removal, the masking tool, the AI Designer, several variations per render, and a higher quality image model. That last one matters here, because this post was made on the free model. What you are looking at is the floor, not the ceiling.

Most tools show you the good version and charge you before you find out which one you were shown. Upload a room and see the free one first.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: Chosen by the user over the advocate's pick, and over the advocate having KILLED it outright. The advocate's kill was that the post either prints the real free cap of 50 a day, landing the reader on a homepage that says 'Free, as often as you like', or drops the number and becomes a myth-fact card with no fact. The first horn is real and was confirmed in source: public/index.html carries an explicit comment that naming the cap reads as a smaller offer, and test/frontend/pricing-copy.test.js pins the ABSENCE of a figure in that key across all eleven language packs. So the number is out. The second horn is what the build answered: the fact is not a number, it is the image. Rendering on gemini-2.5-flash-image makes the post's own proof the thing it is claiming.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The post argues honesty and then spends a paragraph of caption on what free does NOT include, including the admission that the reader is looking at the weaker model. That is the point, but it is also a conversion tax: a reader who wanted to be impressed is told, on the frame that is meant to sell them, that a better version exists behind $11.99. If it underperforms, the diagnosis is almost certainly that paragraph, and the fix is not to delete it but to move it later in the caption, below the fold at 125 characters.

angle: Every other staging post promises the room changes. This one promises the room stays true to the pieces that are not moving, which is the objection that actually stops a seller from trying it.

copy.headline: Stage it with the sofa you are keeping.
copy.caption:
Your sofa is staying with the house. Most virtual staging replaces it anyway, and the buyer finds that out at the showing.

Upload a photo of the piece instead. Up to five pieces. The room gets built around what is actually there.

The sofa in the lower photo is the sofa in the upper one. Same aubergine velvet, same diamond tufting, same low wraparound arms. The walnut tables, the ivory chairs and the brass are ours. The sofa is not.

That is the difference between a staged photo and a fantasy. Only one of them survives the viewing.

Furniture reference upload is a Stagify+ feature. The free tier stages a real room from seven presets, no card asked for.

palette: powder blue tile against white and chrome
topic: brushing one wall and leaving the rest of the photo untouched
angle: Masking Studio changes the region you paint and nothing else. Everything outside the brush is the original photograph rather than a re-render that happens to look similar, which is the claim a whole-photo tool cannot make.
visualSummary: A single deep blue frame holding one photo card of a bathroom, split down the middle by a vertical seam with a drag handle, BEFORE pill on the left and AFTER pill on the right. The room is a white freestanding bath against a large square tiled wall, a chrome floor standing tap rising beside it, two rolled grey towels on the rim, a window throwing daylight from the left. Left of the seam the wall is plain off white ceramic; right of it the same wall is powder blue on the same tile grid. Because both halves are the same photograph, the bath, the tap, the towels and the window run unbroken across the seam and only the tile changes colour. A capsule of copy sits under the card. Powder blue and white against the blue chrome.

copy.headline: One wall. Nothing else.
copy.caption:
We brushed one wall. The bath, the tap and the towels are the same pixels they were before.

That is the whole of Masking Studio. You paint over the part you want changed, and everything outside the brush is left exactly as it was. Not re-rendered, not redrawn. The original file.

The alternative is restaging the whole photo, and that gives you a new room rather than a new wall. The bath moves. The tap grows a second handle. The light from the window lands somewhere else. It all looks fine until you put it next to the picture you started with.

So here is the check. Run your eye across the seam. The bath rim carries straight through it without a step, and the grout lines meet on both sides. Only the tile changes colour.

We measured it rather than trusting it: of the 118,054 pixels outside the brushed area, zero changed.

One photo. One brush. One pass.

Save this for the next time a client asks what a different tile would look like.

generation.note:
The recoloured wall was rendered in Stagify by the account owner and supplied as a finished image, rather than coming from this tool's own mask-edit run. Confirmed product output, so the post advertises Stagify with Stagify's work.

It arrived as a full-frame render: 94.5 per cent of the pixels OUTSIDE the wall differed from the source, worst pixel 721 of 765, and the tap had been redrawn to a different shape. Shipped as delivered it would have made three of the four legend rows false, since they each promise 'the same pixels'. So the supplied wall was composited over the pipeline's own source through the same brush mask: the tile inside the brush is the supplied render, everything outside it is the original photograph, and the delivered frames now differ in exactly one place. The supplied grout grid aligned with the source geometry, so the join carries no seam.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: It is the only shortlisted candidate whose payoff is not resolved on screen. The dorm grid, the tile grid and the plan-to-render all complete at the moment of looking; this one shows a claim you can only check by pointing the tool at your own room, so it earns an open rather than a like. It also answers the objection that actually stops this audience trying AI interiors at all, which is that the tool quietly redecorates things you did not ask about.
devilsAdvocate.whyNotTheOtherFour: i01 and i03 are both one room shown as N variants, the shape of the spare-room deck already in the queue, and both resolve fully on screen. i04 is a near reprint of the 07-30 plan-to-render post. i06 makes a claim about a typed prompt that the frame cannot show without fabricating interface chrome.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The proof is asserted, not shown. With no before frame the headline rests on the caption, and the mask boundary is exactly the geometry that comes back subtly wrong.
devilsAdvocate.howTheRiskLanded: It landed, repeatedly, and drove the whole build. The answer was to stop asserting and start measuring: the delivered frames are diffed pixel by pixel outside the brush, and the before frame was put on the slide beside the after so the viewer can check the claim rather than take it. The final layout is a seam rather than the pins the advocate's brief implied, because the pins tested as confusing.

topic: the compliance line an MLS expects on a staged photo
angle: MLS and NAR rules ask a staged listing photo to say it was staged. Stagify applies that tag before the file leaves the studio, so forgetting it is not a thing the agent can do. The post shows the tag as a real pixel on a real render and spells out how little work it takes: one tick, four looks, a size slider.
visualSummary: One landscape render of a modern dining room on the deep blue field, marked with three numbered brand blue pins and a numbered legend beneath it. The room is a long oak table on a woven charcoal rug under a linear walnut pendant, black dining chairs with ivory boucle seats, a large abstract print in charcoal and cream on the far wall, and a window throwing daylight from the left. Pin one sits on the table top, pin two on the framed print, pin three on the floor beside the dark disclosure chip burnt into the bottom right of the photograph, which reads Virtually staged. A two tone headline sits above the photo and a white CTA pill in the footer.

copy.headline: You cannot forget the label.
copy.caption:
Every staged photo on an MLS has to say it was staged. Ours says it before you download it.

Here is the whole job:

1. Tick "Label as virtually staged" in the staging panel.
2. Pick the look. A dark chip, a light chip, text only, or a band across the foot of the photo.
3. Drag the size if you want it louder.

That is the feature. There is no step four.

The tag is burned into the file, not laid over the preview, so it survives the download, the email and the re upload. And if the tag cannot be applied, you do not get the image. That is on purpose. A photo you believe is labelled and is not is the exact problem the tag exists to prevent.

The dining room here is a real render. The table, the chairs, the rug, the pendant and the print were all generated. The room was empty. The tag in the corner went on by itself.

NAR Article 12 and most MLS rules ask for the same thing: if a listing photo has been altered, say so. Nobody is asking for an essay. Two words in the corner is enough.

First render is free, no card. Link in bio.
